Author: Vivek Bharti Sharma
Bench: Vivek Bharti Sharma
 Office Notes,
 reports,
 orders or

Sl.
 Date or directions Court'S Or Judges'S Order
S No  and  Registrar's  order with  Signatures  14.08.2024 IA/12/2024 (Second Bail Application)

In  CRLA No.62 of 2021  Hon'ble Vivek Bharti Sharma, J.
Present Ms. Divya Jain, learned counsel for the appellant/applicant.
2. Mr. Deepak Bisht, learned Deputy Advocate General for the State.
3. Present criminal appeal has been preferred against the judgment and order dated 19.12.2020 and order dated 21.12.2020 passed by learned Additional District and Sessions Judge/Special Judge(POCSO), Haridwar in Special Session Trial No.33 of 2019, "State Vs. Mukesh"
whereby the appellant/convict has been convicted for the offence under Sections 363,
366(A), 376(2)(n) of IPC and Section 5(l)/6 of the POCSO Act.

4. Heard on second bail application (IA 12 of 2024).
5.

Learned counsel for the appellant/convict would submit that appellant/convict was on bail during the trial and he did not misuse the same; that, the appellant/convict is languishing in jail since 21.12.2020; that, the prosecutrix/victim in her statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C. recorded before the Judicial Magistrate, Haridwar has unequivocally stated that she went with the appellant/convict willingly and the appellant/convict established physical relations with the consent of the prosecutrix/victim; that, the prosecutrix/victim in the medical examination has also stated before the Doctor that she went with the appellant/convict on her own will;
that, the prosecutrix/victim was in love affair with the appellant/convict for the last three years; that, they also established physical relations before 19.11.2018 but 19.11.2018 was the last time when they established physical relations.
CRLA/62/2021 on 14 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125530873/
1

Per contra, Counsel for the State strongly opposed the bail application on the ground that serious allegations of kidnapping and rape have been proved against the appellant/convict, however, he admitted that the appellant/convict was on bail during trial and he did not misuse the same.
7. Having considered the entirety of the facts and without expressing any final opinion on the merits of the case, the appellant/convict is admitted to bail.

8. Let the appellant/convict be released on bail, during the pendency of present criminal appeal, on furnishing bail bond with two sureties in the amount of 40,000/- and personal bond of the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned Trial Court.
9.
Second Bail application (IA 12 of 2024) stands disposed of accordingly.

10. Last but not least, this Court needs to emphasize that investigation in all the criminal matters, especially, offences punishable under POCSO Act, should be conducted with utmost sensitivity, caution and diligence.
It is trite that it is duty of the prosecution to place all the evidences before the trial court, may that be in favour of the prosecution or in favour of the accused.
The State is under legal duty to act in furtherance of the justice.
It goes without saying that no culprit should go unpunished and at the same time no innocent should be convicted because of the unprofessional faulty investigation and laxity in trial.

11. In the present case, when the prosecutrix/victim was examined in the court as a prosecution witness then the prosecutrix/victim stated that she had given statement before the Judicial Magistrate, Haridwar under Section 164 Cr.P.C. in favour of the appellant under the threat of the appellant/convict, it was then the bounden duty of the prosecution to make an application under Section 311 Cr.P.C. to summon the concerned Magistrate for giving the evidentiary value to this statement as the law CRLA/62/2021 on 14 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125530873/
2 mandates, but no such effort was made by the prosecution or the trial court to summon the Judicial Magistrate who had recorded the statement of the prosecutrix/victim in which she had not said anything inculpating the appellant/accused.
12.

Even, it was the duty of the concerned Investigating Officer that if any document is made part of the charge-sheet, such as the statement of the prosecutrix/victim under Section 164 Cr.P.C., then the Investigating Officer should have made the Magistrate a witness in support of his charge-sheet in the present case.
As the statement of the prosecutrix/victim under Section 164 Cr.P.C.
was contradictory to her testimony on oath before the Court, then evidence of Judicial Magistrate becomes important.

13. In view of this Court, the Investigating Officer has also failed in discharging his duties and so has the Government Counsel, who had concluded the evidence of the prosecution and advanced the arguments, by not making an application under Section 311 Cr.P.C.(as the then Criminal Procedure Code) to summon the Magistrate as a witness.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sidhartha Vashisht Vs. State (NCT of Delhi) (2010) 6 SCC 1 has defined the Role of Public Prosecutor and his duty of disclosure, which is extracted as under:-
"Role of Public Prosecutor and his duty of disclosure 184.

entities.text: Sidhartha Vashisht Vs. State (NCT of Delhi) (2010) 6 SCC 1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is thus important for us to address the role of a Prosecutor, disclosure requirements if placed by the Prosecutor and the role of a Judge in a criminal trial.
185. A Public Prosecutor is appointed under Section 24 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Thus, Public Prosecutor is a statutory office of high regard.

This Court has observed the role of a Prosecutor in Shiv Kumar v. Hukam Chand (1999) 7 SCC 467:
1999 SCC (Cri) 1277) as follows: (SCC.
p. 472, para 13) "13.

entities.text:
Shiv Kumar v. Hukam Chand (1999) 7 SCC 467:
1999 SCC (Cri) 1277)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: From the scheme of the Code the legislative intention is manifestly clear that prosecution in a Sessions Court cannot be conducted by anyone other than the Public Prosecutor.
The legislature reminds the State that the policy must strictly conform to fairness in the trial of an accused in a Sessions Court.
A Public Prosecutor is not expected to show a thirst to reach the case in the conviction of the accused somehow or the other irrespective of the true facts involved in the case.
The expected attitude of the Public Prosecutor while conducting prosecution must be couched in fairness not only to the court and to the investigating agencies but to the accused as well.
If an accused is entitled to any legitimate benefit during trial the Public Prosecutor should not scuttle/conceal it.
On the contrary, it is the duty of the Public Prosecutor to winch it to the force and make it available to the accused.
Even if the defence counsel overlooked it, the Public Prosecutor has the added responsibility to bring it to the notice of the court if it comes to his knowledge.
A private counsel, if allowed a free hand to conduct prosecution would focus on bringing the case to conviction even if it is not a fit case to be so convicted.

That is the reason why Parliament applied a CRLA/62/2021 on 14 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125530873/
3 bridle on him and subjected his role strictly to the instructions given by the Public Prosecutor."
186. This Court has also held that the Prosecutor does not represent the investigating agencies, but the State.
This Court in Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra (1994) 4 SCC 602: 1994 SCC (Cri) 1087) held: (SCC pp. 630-31, para 23) "23.

entities.text: Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra (1994) 4 SCC 602: 1994 SCC (Cri) 1087)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A Public Prosecutor is an important officer of the State Government and is appointed by the State under the Criminal Procedure Code.
He is not a part of the investigating agency.
He is an independent statutory authority.

The public prosecutor is expected to independently apply his mind to the request of the investigating agency before submitting a report to the court for extension of time with view to enable the investigating agency to complete the investigation.
He is not merely a post office or a forwarding agency.

A Public Prosecutor may or may not agree with the reasons given by the investigating officer for seeking extension of time and may find that the investigation had not progressed in the proper manner or that there has been unnecessary, deliberate or avoidable delay in completing the investigation."
187.

Therefore, a Public Prosecutor has wider set of duties than to merely ensure that the accused is punished, the duties of ensuring fair play in the proceedings, all relevant facts are brought before the court in order for the determination of truth and justice for all the parties including the victims.

It must be noted that these duties do not allow the Prosecutor to be lax in any of his duties as against the accused."
14.

This Court would not hesitate to say that even Trial Court has failed to summon the witness by exercising its power under Section 311 Cr.P.C.(as the Criminal Procedure Law was) and now Section 348 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which is extracted hereunder:-
"348. Power to summon material witness, or examine person present.--Any Court may, at any stage of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Sanhita,
summon any person as a witness, or examine any person in attendance, though not summoned as a witness, or re- call and re-examine any person already examined; and the Court shall summon and examine or re-call and re- examine any such person if his evidence appears to it to be essential to the just decision of the case."

15. It goes without saying that the trial court is under duty to summon the important witnesses under Section 311 Cr.P.C. (The Criminal Procedure as then was) and the trial court also has the power to summon any witness before it, who is conversant with the fact.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Zahira Habibullah Sheikh (5) v. State of Gujarat, (2006) 3 SCC 374: (2006) 2 SCC (Crl) 8: 2006 SCC OnLine SC 277 at page 392 has settled the law as under:-
"28.

entities.text: Zahira Habibullah Sheikh (5) v. State of Gujarat, (2006) 3 SCC 374: (2006) 2 SCC (Crl) 8: 2006 SCC OnLine SC 277
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: As indicated above, the section is wholly discretionary.
The second part of it imposes upon the Magistrate an obligation it is, that the court shall summon and examine all persons whose evidence appears to be essential to the just decision of the case.
It is a cardinal rule in the law of evidence that the best available evidence should be brought before the court.
Sections 60, 64 and 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872 (in short "the Evidence Act") are based on this rule.

The court is not empowered under CRLA/62/2021 on 14 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125530873/
4 the provisions of the Code to compel either the prosecution or the defence to examine any particular witness or witnesses on their side.
This must be left to the parties.
But in weighing the evidence, the court can take note of the fact that the best available evidence has not been given, and can draw an adverse inference.
The court will often have to depend on intercepted allegations made by the parties, or on inconclusive inference from facts elicited in the evidence.
In such cases, the court has to act under the second part of the section.
Sometimes the examination of witnesses as directed by the court may result in what is thought to be "filling of loopholes".
That is purely a subsidiary factor and cannot be taken into account.

Whether the new evidence is essential or not must of course depend on the facts of each case, and has to be determined by the Presiding Judge.
29.
The object of Section 311 is to bring on record evidence not only from the point of view of the accused and the prosecution but also from the point of view of the orderly society....."
16. Thus, it is trite to say that Section 311 Cr.P.C. imposes an obligation upon the Court to summon important witnesses essential to the just decision of the case.
It is cardinal rule in the law of evidence that the best available evidence should be brought before the Court.
The object of Section 311 Cr.P.C. is to bring evidence not only from the point of view of the accused or the prosecution but also necessary in the larger interest of the society and State.
17. In the considered view of this Court, this measure would help in the dispensation of justice to one and all, may that be the State or the accused of the offence.

18. A copy of this order be sent to all the Courts of the State and also be sent to the Principal Secretary (Law), Government of Uttarakhand to take appropriate action to preclude the instances of negligence by prosecutors in prosecution in the Trial Court by not moving an application under Section 311 Cr.P.C. to summon all important witnesses whether named in list of witnesses or not,
whose evidence is necessary to bring all the important facts and evidence on record of trial court.
19.
The copy of this order also be circulated among all Government Counsel (Criminal) and Prosecution Officers of the State.

20. List this case on 27.12.2024 for final hearing.
(Vivek Bharti Sharma, J.) 14.08.2024 SS CRLA/62/2021 on 14 August, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/125530873/
